edits.quote: Cover each shape with blue blocks in a different way on each copy. Draw around the blocks to show each way. (3 copies of the small hexagon, 4 copies of the 2-long hexagon, and on page 4, 5 copies of the 3-long hexagon)
edits.fix: Each shape has exactly one fewer covering than it has copies (2, 3 and 4 coverings), so 'a different way on each copy' cannot be done and a child will keep hunting for a way that does not exist. Reword to 'Find all the different ways to cover each shape with blue blocks. Draw each way on a copy.' and add a 'How many ways?' box beside each shape. Keep the spare copy on purpose or remove it.

edits.quote: Five copies of the 3-long hexagon stacked with gaps of about 1/6 inch
edits.fix: Space the copies out, or drop to four copies as part of the P3 fix, so that a child drawing around blocks on one copy does not run onto the next copy.

edits.quote: Cover each shape with yellow, red, blue and green blocks.
edits.fix: Change to 'with any of these blocks'. As written, a child may think every color has to be used, and the best cover of the small triangle uses 3 reds only (the minimums are 3, 6 and 5).

edits.quote: How many? (box under yes/no for every shape, including the 2x yellow hexagon and the 2x purple chevron, which cannot be made from 4 of their own pieces)
edits.fix: Relabel the box 'If yes, how many?' or drop it. Two of the four answers are 'no', and for those 'How many?' has no answer.

edits.quote: The 2x purple chevron alone at the top of page 7; the bottom two-thirds of the page is blank
edits.fix: Use the empty space for one or two more scaled shapes, such as a 2x blue rhombus (4 blues) or a 3x green triangle (9 greens), so the page break does not leave a mostly blank sheet.

edits.quote: first player won / second player won (empty boxes under each board)
edits.fix: Say in the problem text that partners play each board several times and make a mark for the winner of each game. Otherwise the purpose of the boxes is unclear.
Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

k-1.summary: A substantial, correct K–1 set at actual size: impossible covers (the 4-triangle triangle and a 12-triangle trapezoid), fewest greens (2, 3, 4), all ways to cover growing hexagons (2, 3, 4), fewest blocks (3, 6, 5, where using yellow first fails), scaled shapes (green and red yes, yellow and purple no), and a strategy game (second player wins on the hexagon, first player wins on both strips). The main fix is P3: it asks for a different covering on every copy, but every shape has one more copy than it has coverings. The rest are small wording fixes in P4–P6 and a mostly empty page 7.

edits.quote: Each board is the big hexagon with two small triangles cut out (the black ones).
edits.fix: Delete. The diagrams already show this, and the shared rules already say black triangles may not be covered. Start the problem at 'Which boards can be covered with blue rhombuses?'
Delete. 'Cover each triangle with purple chevrons and green triangles' already says this.

edits.quote: Then fill in the table on the next page to compare purple chevrons with blue rhombuses on the same triangles.
edits.fix: Cut this directed comparison step. Keep the table as plain recording space and let the closing question ('Could purple chevrons ever need fewer greens than blue rhombuses, on any board at all? Explain.') carry the problem.

edits.quote: Table column '6 on each side' / 'Greens with blue rhombuses'
edits.fix: No problem asks children to cover a size-6 triangle with blues: P2 uses sizes 3, 4 and 5, and P4 uses size 7. Either change P2's third triangle to size 6, or say that the size-6 board is also to be covered with blues. With chevrons the answers are 5, 4 and 8; with blues they are 3, 4 and 6.
Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

grades-2-3.summary: The strongest band. It develops the up/down counting obstruction in a well-chosen order, and every answer checks out: possible and impossible boards (A yes, B no, C no, D yes), fewest greens (3, 4, 5), hexagons with holes (a and c yes, b and d no), a proof for the size-7 triangle (7), chevrons against rhombi, balanced 9/9 boards that still need 2 and 4 greens because of a local imbalance, and an inverse design problem (best answer 7 triangles). The only edits are P5's wordy directions and a table column whose blue-rhombus value no problem asks for.

edits.quote: Give your six ways of covering hexagon C the numbers 1 to 6. (and 'Way 1' to 'Way 6' answer lines in P3 on page 4)
edits.fix: This gives away the count of 6 that P1 asks children to justify ('explain how you know you have found every way'). Change to 'Number your ways of covering hexagon C' and use unnumbered answer lines in P3.

edits.quote: the rhombus sitting on the bottom edge lies flat, so its top edge is flat too. The rhombus sitting on that edge also lies flat, and so on up to the top edge of the hexagon.
edits.fix: 'Lies flat' clashes with the shared rule 'Blocks lie flat inside the outline'. Rewrite as one sentence: the rhombuses with a flat (horizontal) top and bottom edge form a chain from the bottom edge to the top edge, as shaded in the picture. Then define R and L. The picture (R L R R on a 1-3-1 hexagon) is correct.

edits.quote: Write the points you flipped, in order, and the number of flips.
edits.fix: Shorten to 'List the points in order.' The 'Points flipped:' and 'Flips:' fields already ask for the rest.

edits.quote: Single size-2 hexagon board with 'Number of ways:' box and blank half page; no copies to draw on
edits.fix: Add a page of half-size copies of the hexagon, or a triangular grid, so children can record the 20 coverings they build. Freehand hexagons are unusable for an exhaustive count.
Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

grades-4-5.summary: A deep and correct development of kernel 2, with every diagram and answer checked: all coverings of small hexagons (2, 3, 6), the flip map for hexagon C (the farthest pair is 4 flips apart), chain letters that fix the covering and swap an adjacent RL pair on each flip, counts 10, 20 and 70, fewest-flip puzzles (2, 6 and 8 flips, where 8 is the full-cube extreme), and the even-round-trip parity question. The fixes are: stop giving away the count of six before P1 asks for justification, rewrite the 'lies flat' chain paragraph, trim a duplicated recording direction, and add drawing copies for P7's 20 coverings.

overall.strongest: Grades 2–3 takes the up/down counting obstruction from first examples through proofs, the chevron comparison, local obstructions on balanced boards and an inverse design problem, and every answer is correct.
overall.weakest: K–1 P3 cannot be finished as written because each shape has one more copy than it has coverings, and K–1 P5 asks 'How many?' for two shapes that cannot be made from their own pieces.
